Prime Minister Andy Burnham met with European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on Friday to secure a reset of post Brexit relations through new agreements on food exports, emissions trading, and youth mobility. The agreed sanitary and phytosanitary arrangement removes most post Brexit checks and restrictions on British food and agricultural products starting March 1, 2028, in exchange for the United Kingdom following specified European Union regulations. The two sides also agreed to link their emissions trading systems beginning in January 2028. A youth experience scheme will permit up to 100,000 young citizens from both jurisdictions to live and work abroad for up to three years.

Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by Yemen's Houthi militia toward Riyadh early Saturday, following an earlier Houthi strike that damaged the Public Investment Fund tower and neighboring buildings in the capital. The coalition fighting the Houthis stated that its forces targeted operational capabilities at Hodeidah port used in smuggling operations and weapons transport, alongside military targets in Sanaa, Saada, and Taiz governorates. The Houthi military spokesman asserted that the operation successfully hit vital targets in Riyadh. Independent observers noted potential impacts on the proposed United States and Saudi Arabia nuclear power pact.

NATO aircraft scrambled in response to three objects breaching Polish airspace overnight during a large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine that killed at least five people and damaged three bridges in Kyiv. Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz stated that the objects included an Kh-101 cruise missile, another missile, and a jet-powered drone. The Kh-101 missile came down in a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec, about 30 miles from the Ukrainian border and approximately 47 miles from where military exercises were underway. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk characterized the incursion as an intentional Russian provocation, and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte condemned the event.

The International Court of Justice found Myanmar responsible for state-sponsored genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during a 2017 military campaign, marking the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide in the court history. Delivered in The Hague by court president Iwasawa Yuji, the ruling was decided by a majority vote of nine to six in a case brought by The Gambia. The court accepted estimates that at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, along with documentation of systematic sexual violence and village burnings. The United Nations court ordered Myanmar to provide safe passage home for refugees, issue reparations, and prosecute individuals involved.

Danish authorities announced on Friday that they thwarted a plot by Russian intelligence services to assassinate Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev, during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb on September 25. Police arrested three men traveling in a car carrying firearms and knives near the venue, with two suspects tied to the gang Loyal to Familia charged with attempted murder and assisting foreign intelligence. In response, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen summoned the Russian ambassador and announced the expulsion of Russia's defense attaché with a seven-day deadline to leave the country. Russian state media asserted that the accusations lacked evidence.

A federal jury in Los Angeles convicted 30-year-old Jonathan Rinderknecht on Friday of two counts of federal arson for starting the Palisades Fire, which killed 12 people and destroyed over 6,800 structures in January 2025. Jurors returned the guilty verdict on the third day of deliberations in the second trial after a previous jury deadlocked ten to two in favor of acquittal, resulting in a mistrial declared by Judge Anne Hwang in June. Prosecutors presented digital forensic evidence, cell phone location tracking, and ChatGPT search history regarding fire liability during the retrial. The defense argued that holiday fireworks served as the alternative source of ignition.

The removal of coal, oil, and gas from the text sparked intense pushback from the European Union, France, and Panama at the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, where Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro threatened to block any final agreement. Co-hosted by Turkey and Australia, the conference faced severe criticism from civil society organizations and 100 environmental groups warning it was on course to become one of the most disappointing climate summits in decades. Peru's delegation blamed geopolitical divisions between oil producers and European delegates for the plenary deadlock. The talks extended into overtime on Saturday as delegates debated the draft text.

US Vice President JD Vance declined to say whether he would have authorized military strikes against Iran during a White House press briefing alongside President Donald Trump on Friday. Vance stated that the decision belonged to the president and described his job as supporting the president of the United States. President Trump said he was not unhappy with Vance's assessment but wanted stronger support, arguing that the vice president should recognize the necessity of the military operation. Vance previously attributed Republican midterm election losses to the Iran conflict in a social media post.

SpaceX retained a team of five Washington lobbyists from Mehlman Consulting with close ties to the Democratic Party starting October 1, coinciding with polling projections for the midterm elections. Following their victory in securing 228 seats in the House of Representatives and 54 seats in the Senate, Democratic lawmakers plan to launch oversight inquiries into Elon Musk's business operations and government contracts. The planned probes will examine restrictions imposed on Starlink and Starshield in Ukraine alongside Pentagon contracts. Elon Musk recently traveled to China for the APEC summit and appeared in state-controlled videos encouraging American tourism.

The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals issued an administrative stay on Friday, indefinitely pausing the Environmental Protection Agency permit that allowed the US Army to conduct controlled detonations of nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. The emergency ruling follows a lawsuit filed on Thursday by Earthjustice on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa chapter. The petition argued that federal agencies failed to adequately assess environmental and safety risks. The Army had postponed the originally scheduled Friday detonation to Monday before the court intervention. ===AUDIO_SCRIPT===

## OPINION | International Courts Lack Teeth When Sovereignty Meets Atrocities
A: This is Void Opinion. Through a pragmatic lens today. International courts lack teeth when sovereignty meets atrocities.
A: The International Court of Justice delivered a binding verdict in The Hague holding Myanmar responsible for state-sponsored genocide against the Rohingya minority. Court president Iwasawa Yuji announced the nine to six majority decision in the case brought by the United Nations body by The Gambia. The documentation includes one thousand eight hundred thirty-four acts of rape alongside the systematic destruction of villages. The tribunal ordered Myanmar to permit the safe return of displaced refugees, disburse reparations, and prosecute individuals suspected of orchestrating the atrocities. Government officials in Myanmar dismissed the ruling as unfair and claimed the nation was unjustly accused.
A: International jurisprudence operates on the fiction that states care about their standing in global forums more than their monopoly on internal violence. We watch tribunals issue binding orders while domestic apparatuses dismiss the findings without consequence. The court has accepted specific metrics of human destruction, yet it possesses no enforcement mechanism to compel the prosecution of military commanders or the payment of reparations. When a judicial body documents thousands of rapes and tens of thousands of deaths, the resulting mandate asks a defiant government to police itself. We cannot build an international order that relies on the voluntary compliance of regimes that proved their willingness to commit mass murder.
A: Pragmatism requires us to look past the moral clarity of the judgment and examine the institutional void surrounding it. Civil society groups now demand economic and military sanctions against the state, pushing international actors to bridge the gap between legal accountability and enforcement. Yet those same external actors remain divided over whether circumstantial evidence sufficiently establishes genocidal intent under strict legal standards. The narrow nine to six vote at the court reflects this deep procedural friction. International law must balance the necessity of punishing atrocities against the reality of sovereign resistance. When courts reach for universal justice without the coercive power to back it up, the verdict risks becoming an empty registry of grief.
A: We must decide whether international justice functions as a deterrent or merely a retrospective archive of human suffering. The court demands that refugees return to the sites of their displacement under the protection of the very forces that drove them out. That demand ignores the physical reality on the ground in Rakhine State. Real institutions require enforcement to survive, and until we build the architecture to compel compliance, judicial declarations will remain monuments to our highest aspirations and our deepest impotence.

## CLOSE
A: That's On Air from Void News. Nine thousand seven hundred pounds of unstable lead azide remain paused in Middletown, Iowa, pending further court review. Every source, every story, at Void News.
